deep.reconstruction:
This page has no derivation. It is a fair-copy excerpt or summary of the opening of a printed article: Astronomische Nachrichten No. 983, 'Über Projection von Land- und Himmelskarten, von Herrn Dr. C. [Bremiker?]'. The author's name is underlined and hard to read. 'Bremiker' (Carl Bremiker, Berlin astronomer and maker of star charts) fits the letter shapes but is not certain. The page is therefore not original Riemann mathematics but reading notes or a copy. Its content is a historical introduction to conformal ('in den kleinsten Theilen ähnlich') map projection, in five points:

(1) Lambert (1772, 'Anmerkungen und Zusätze zur Entwerfung der Land- und Himmelscharten') first imposed the condition of similarity in the smallest parts (conformality). He expressed it as a differential equation. He showed that the stereographic and Mercator projections satisfy it and that many more do. In modern terms, with latitude φ, longitude λ and isometric latitude q = log tan(π/4 + φ/2), the sphere's metric is cos^2φ (dq^2 + dλ^2). Hence a map (x, y) is conformal iff x + i y = f(q + i λ) (or of q − iλ) with f holomorphic.

(2) Lagrange integrated this equation, so there are infinitely many conformal projections (one for each holomorphic f).

(3) The most common projections other than the stereographic are not conformal. Those named are Flamsteed (sinusoidal), De l'Isle (equidistant conic), Senex, Bonne and Murdoch. The text says they give only 'Zerrbilder' (distorted images) that worsen toward the edge of the map, and sets them aside.

(4) Lagrange, in a Berlin Academy memoir of 1779 ('Sur la construction des cartes géographiques'), solved conformal projection of the ellipsoid of revolution with all meridians and parallels mapped to circles. In modern form the solution is w = (a ζ^n + b)/(c ζ^n + d), where ζ = exp(q + iλ) and q is the ellipsoidal isometric latitude. The excerpted author announces he will show this projection is 'not the only one': infinitely many share the property, although Lagrange's derivation suggests uniqueness.

(5) Gauss, in Schumacher's Astronomische Abhandlungen, Heft 3 (1825; the 1822 Copenhagen prize essay), showed that conformal mapping of any surface onto any other reduces to Lagrange's equation. In modern terms, both metrics are brought to isothermal form and the map is a holomorphic function of the isothermal coordinate. The page breaks off with '..'.
errors: No mathematical errors, since no computations are performed.

Historical nuance: Lagrange's 1779 result is a multi-parameter family (powers of ζ composed with Möbius transformations), not literally a single projection. The excerpted author's claim of 'infinitely many' is therefore partly a matter of how Lagrange's parameters are counted.
Lambert himself had already produced several conformal projections (conformal conic, transverse Mercator), not just the observation that stereographic and Mercator are conformal.

transcription_corrections: The author's name in line 2-3 is underlined and partly legible; it plausibly reads 'Bremiker' (Dr. C. Bremiker), not unreadable.
'gewinnen erst mit Lambert' is likely 'gewannen erst mit Lambert ... eine festere Basis' (the verb in the image looks like 'gewinnen'/'gewannen'; the grammar requires a plural subject understood).
The final word read as 'Vergleichung[?]' is more likely 'Gleichung' or 'Vergleichung' in the sense of 'equation'; its referent is Lagrange's equation.
The trailing '..' marks the copyist's abbreviation of the article's continuation.
